evals.prompt:
can you tear apart my deck before I send it? I'm emailing a DocSend link to about 15 seed investors on Thursday and I only get one shot. I can't attach the PDF from my phone so here's the text of every slide, in order. Be honest.

SLIDE 1
GAPWREN
The Future of Clinic Scheduling

SLIDE 2
THE PROBLEM
Cancellations are killing independent PT clinics
- Last-minute cancellations are a massive problem
- Front desks are overwhelmed
- Revenue walks out the door every day

SLIDE 3
THE SOLUTION
An AI-powered, end-to-end scheduling platform
- Smart Waitlist
- Auto-Fill Engine
- Insights Hub

SLIDE 4
WHY NOW
AI is transforming healthcare

SLIDE 5
TRACTION
Strong early momentum
- 3 clinics in pilot
- 40+ clinics on the waitlist
- At my own clinic we filled 61 of 148 cancelled slots in the first 10 weeks

SLIDE 6
THE MARKET
$12B TAM
- 38,000 outpatient PT clinics in the US
- If we capture just 1% we're a $120M business

SLIDE 7
THE COMPETITION
(table: rows = Text-based waitlist, Auto-fill, Insurance check, PT-specific. Columns = Gapwren, Mendwren, Kestrel Scheduler, generic practice software. Gapwren has a check in every row, the others have one or two.)
Gapwren is the first and only AI scheduling platform built for PT.

SLIDE 8
BUSINESS MODEL
Flexible SaaS pricing for clinics of every size

SLIDE 9
TEAM
Me (founder, physical therapist, owned a 4-therapist clinic for 9 years) plus 2 advisors from big health systems

SLIDE 10
THE ASK
We're raising our seed round. Join us.

SLIDE 11
Thank you! Questions?
evals.expected_output: A written review in the skill's fixed order, not a rewritten deck. It opens with a verdict of three lines or fewer: not ready, the one fix, and what is needed from the founder. It states the reading: a sent-ahead seed deck scored on the investor column, and says the review covers pasted text only, so look and legibility are not scored and the rendered-and-read gate is open. It records what already works, naming the founder's own number (61 of 148 cancelled slots filled in 10 weeks at the founder's clinic) and the nine years owning a clinic. It shows the skim read (the largest lines in order) and says they are category labels that carry no argument. It gives a score out of the points still available (94 on the investor column) with the arithmetic by line, and says a deck for investors with no price and no definite ask is not ready to send whatever the total. It marks gates as tripped: the unsourced $12B figure and the one percent reasoning, the unchecked 'first and only' claim, and unsourced statements about the named competitors Mendwren and Kestrel Scheduler in the tick grid. It explains why the tick grid loses a reader and offers the alternatives-by-kind form plus a concede-then-claim answer, without recommending a map that puts Gapwren alone in the best corner. It flags: no price, an ask with no amount or milestone, a waitlist and pilots worded as traction, invented names for product parts (Smart Waitlist, Auto-Fill Engine, Insights Hub), a why-now with no date or source, advisors on the team slide, and ending on 'Thank you'. It lists questions the deck does not answer (who pays, what a clinic costs to serve, how the first outside clinics arrive, how the raise amount is derived), while the message to the founder carries five questions or fewer. Fixes come with replacement wording, including claim headlines built only from figures that are in the deck, for example a problem or proof headline using 61 of 148 slots. Any replacement needing a fact the founder did not give (price, raise amount, milestone, the source for 38,000 clinics) uses a placeholder such as [NEED: ...] and appears in a 'Numbers to find' list. The body of the review ends with the one fix that matters most. It invents no numbers, proposes no specific price or raise amount as fact, gives no invest or pass verdict, and says the score measures craft and evidence and is not a forecast of funding.

evals.prompt:
ok so I need a pitch deck and I've never made one. sorry this is a brain dump, I'm dictating while I drive.

I ran restaurant kitchens for 14 years, last 6 as kitchen manager at a 120 seat place. The thing that always killed us was the temperature logs. Health department wants the walk-in and every reach-in logged twice a day on paper, and nobody does it, people just pencil in numbers at the end of the week. We got written up in 2022 because the log said 38 degrees all week and the inspector's thermometer said 46. Lost about 2,300 dollars of product that day and had a re-inspection.

So I built this thing, it's called Chillfinch. Little sensors in the coolers, they log by themselves, and the app texts the manager when something drifts. My cousin wrote the app, he's a real developer but he's part time on it, nights and weekends. We started in January. It's been running at my old restaurant since May and at my friend's taco place since July, nobody pays yet, I gave them the sensors. Since May it's caught 9 drifts at my old place and one of them was a compressor dying on a Saturday night, they saved the whole walk-in.

The part where it writes the health department report for you automatically, that's not done yet, that's what my cousin is on now. Also want to do predicting when a compressor is about to fail but that's way later.

Sensors cost me 31 bucks each and a kitchen needs like 4. The data plan thing is about 11 a month per restaurant. I don't know what to charge, maybe 30 a month? or 99? no idea.

I think we're basically the first ones doing this with AI for independent restaurants, the big chains have expensive systems but nobody does it for the little guys.

I want to raise like half a million, maybe a million, to hire my cousin full time and get to, I don't know, a few hundred restaurants. Also there's a food tech accelerator with applications due in two weeks, I want to send them something too.

Can you just make the deck?
evals.expected_output: A first response that moves the work forward without inventing anything. It settles the deck kind before writing: it notices two readers (investors by email and an accelerator application due in two weeks), says which it is building first and why, or states that assumption plainly, and notes the application version is a shorter cut from the same outline. It plays back what it understood in a few lines so the founder can correct it. It sorts the ramble into a claims ledger: sensor logging and drift texts run today; the automatic health department report is being built; compressor failure prediction is later, and it keeps the report feature out of present tense and the prediction feature off the product slides. It keeps the founder's own numbers and tags them as the founder's: 14 years, the 2022 write-up with 38 logged against 46 measured, about $2,300 of product lost, started in January, in use at two restaurants since May and July, 9 drifts caught, the Saturday compressor case as the old-way against new-way example, $31 a sensor, about 4 per kitchen, about $11 a month per restaurant. It asks five or fewer numbered questions that only the founder can answer, with assumptions written as statements, and asks nothing the dictation already answers. For price it brings a worked range built from the cost figures given (hardware of about $124 per kitchen and about $11 a month to serve) and asks the founder to pick. For the ask it asks for one amount or for a milestone and timeline, shows that the raise must reconcile with price and customer count, and does not choose between half a million and a million. It does not accept 'first' or 'nobody does it for the little guys' as a claim: it says a prior-art check is needed and offers the narrower true statement to use meanwhile. It includes a headline outline of roughly 10 to 15 slides for a sent deck in a pitch order, where every headline is a claim and none is a category title, built only from the founder's numbers, with placeholders such as [NEED: monthly price] where a fact is missing and a 'Numbers to find' list at the end. The stage is stated once in positive, exact words (in daily use at two restaurants since May), with no slide line such as 'no revenue yet' and no claim of customers, revenue or pilots that do not exist. No market size figure, competitor fact, price or raise amount is invented. It does not hand back a blank template.

evals.prompt:
I asked another AI to write a pitch deck outline for my company and it gave me the thing below. It looks impressive but something feels off and I can't tell what. Can you clean it up into something I can actually email to investors?

Context so you know what's real: Dockwren is a dock scheduling tool for small regional warehouses. Two warehouses use it for free right now, mine and my brother-in-law's. No paying customers. One developer, part time. The AI dock assignment feature is designed but not built, right now a person drags trucks onto docks on a screen. I have not decided pricing. I ran a 60,000 square foot warehouse for 12 years.

Here's what the AI gave me:

Slide 1: Title. Dockwren: The Operating System for the Modern Dock
Slide 2: The Problem. Warehouses waste 37% of labor hours on dock congestion. Detention fees cost the industry $1.3B a year.
Slide 3: The Solution. Three pillars: Orchestrate, Optimize, Observe.
Slide 4: Why Now. AI and the supply chain crisis have created a once-in-a-generation opportunity.
Slide 5: Product. AI dock assignment automatically assigns every truck to the best dock in real time.
Slide 6: Traction. Validated: 42% faster truck turnaround in pilots. Strong pipeline of design partners.
Slide 7: Market. TAM $48B, SAM $6.2B, SOM $310M.
Slide 8: Competition. 2x2 matrix, axes Reactive vs Predictive and Single Site vs Network. Dockwren alone in the top right. Dockwren is the first and only AI-native dock platform for SMB warehouses.
Slide 9: Business Model. Starter $89/mo, Pro $249/mo, unlimited docks and unlimited trucks on every plan.
Slide 10: Go To Market. Content, SEO, partnerships, paid social, outbound and channel resellers.
Slide 11: The Ask. Raising $2M to reach 500 warehouses and $3M ARR in 12 months. Use of funds: 50% product, 30% sales and marketing, 15% operations.
evals.expected_output: An import-mode response: it treats the outline as structure to improve and never as a source, and it does not score it, because an outline is not a deck. It opens with three lines or fewer that answer what feels off: the outline is built on numbers and claims nobody gave it. It says what is worth keeping (the overall order, one topic per slide) and then lists every number and claim in the outline with a tag: confirmed by the founder, sourced, or unsupported. It marks as unsupported and removes or replaces with placeholders: 37% of labor hours, $1.3B in detention fees, the TAM, SAM and SOM ladder, and the 42% faster turnaround, and it says 'validated', 'pilots' and 'pipeline of design partners' cannot stay because the founder has two free users and no pilots. It runs the ask arithmetic and shows it: 500 x $249 x 12 = $1,494,000, about half of $3M (and $534,000 at $89); reaching $3M from 500 warehouses needs $500 a month each, or about 1,005 warehouses at $249; and 50 + 30 + 15 = 95, so the use of funds does not add up. It flags 'first and only' and 'operating system' as ranking claims that need a prior-art check, and offers a narrower true line to use meanwhile. It flags the 2x2 with Dockwren alone in the top right as the same move as a tick grid and proposes alternatives by kind with a concede-then-claim answer, with named competitors moved to an appendix with sources. It moves AI dock assignment out of present tense because the founder said it is designed and not built, and describes what runs today (a person drags trucks onto docks on a screen). It replaces the pillar names with plain verbs. It says the $89 and $249 unlimited tiers are proposals that need a cost-to-serve check and the founder's decision, and does not print them. It replaces the six-channel go-to-market list with a question about the one real route to the first outside warehouses. It rewrites the outline as claim headlines in a pitch order using only the founder's real facts (two warehouses in daily use, 12 years running a 60,000 square foot warehouse, one part-time developer), with [NEED: ...] placeholders elsewhere and a 'Numbers to find' list. It states the stage once in positive, exact words and writes no line about what the company lacks. It asks five or fewer questions that only the founder can answer, such as a count from their own use, the price inputs, and the raise amount with its milestone, and asks nothing the founder's context already answers. It invents no replacement numbers.

evals.prompt: Attached is the PDF of my seed deck draft for Gapwren (gapwren-seed-draft.pdf). It goes out by email to investors next week. My co-founder looked it over and says it's clean and the titles are all proper claims now. Can you give it a real review before I send it?
evals.expected_output: A review made from the rendered file. It says it rendered and read all six pages and read the text layer in order, and it gives type sizes or text order as the evidence for what it finds. It reports three things that pasted text would not show. (1) A category tag ('THE PROBLEM', 'THE SOLUTION', 'PROOF', 'THE COMPETITION', 'THE ASK') sits above the headline on slides 2 to 6. Each is small (about 10 pt, under a 30 pt headline and smaller than the 14 pt body) and is still the first text line of its page, so a model or a screening tool reads it as the title. The fix is to delete the tags, not to shrink them. (2) On slide 4 the largest text is '2,400' at about 96 pt, roughly three times the headline. It is the founder's career patient count, not the number the headline is about (61 of 148 cancelled slots), and a skimmer can take it for product usage. The fix is to make the product's own number the large figure, or to label the career total as the founder's and set it smaller. (3) The table on slide 5 is a tick grid even though the alternatives' cells hold text and honest blanks: Gapwren's column is all ticks while every other column has a blank. It proposes alternatives by kind with what each leaves undone, plus a concede-then-claim answer, and does not propose a map with Gapwren alone in the best corner. Under what already works it records that the headlines are claims built from the founder's own numbers and that the ask reconciles, with the sums shown: 120 x $180 x 12 = $259,200; $600,000 / 18 = about $33,333 a month; $280,000 + $200,000 + $120,000 = $600,000. It raises what the deck leaves open for an investor as questions or placeholders and not as invented content: no market arithmetic, no cost-to-serve check behind the $180 price, no route to the first paying clinics, and a sample-data screen as the only product image. It follows the fixed review order with a score on the investor column, opens with a verdict of three lines or fewer, ends the body on one fix, invents no numbers, and gives no invest or pass verdict.

evals.prompt:
I showed my Chillfinch deck to a friend who angel invests and I also pasted it into another AI. Their notes are under the deck. Can you apply the feedback and give me the next version of the outline? It goes out by email to seed investors.

DECK (the headline of each slide)
1. Chillfinch logs every cooler in a restaurant kitchen and texts the manager when one drifts. (small label: Pre-launch. In daily use at two restaurants since May.)
2. A paper temperature log said 38 degrees all week while the walk-in sat at 46
3. Sensors log each cooler on their own and text the manager when one drifts
4. One Saturday night a dying compressor was caught before the walk-in was lost
5. Nine drifts caught at one restaurant since May (strip: Done, logging and drift texts, May. Now, the health department report, in build. Next, the first paying kitchens.)
6. Kitchens log by hand because the chains' systems cost more than a small kitchen can pay
7. $59 a month per kitchen, plus $124 of sensors up front
8. We are raising a seed round to reach our first paying kitchens

FEEDBACK
A. (friend) Your ask is mush. Say: raising $750K to go from 25 pilot kitchens to 300 paying restaurants and $500K ARR in 12 months.
B. (friend) Add a market slide. Cold chain monitoring is an $8.2B market, lead with that.
C. (AI) Slide 1 should position you as the only AI-native food safety platform for independent restaurants.
D. (AI) Replace slide 6 with a feature comparison grid against the chain systems so investors can see you win on every row.
E. (AI) Lead with the automatic health department report, it's your most impressive feature.
F. (friend) Slide 4 is your best slide. Don't touch it.
evals.expected_output: A response that reviews before rebuilding and sorts each of the six points into taken, changed or declined, with the reason. A: right about form (the ask needs one amount, a countable milestone and a date) and unreliable on the figures. It shows the arithmetic: 300 x $59 x 12 = $212,400, which is $287,600 short of $500,000; reaching $500,000 takes about $139 a month from each of 300 kitchens, or about 707 kitchens at $59. It says '25 pilot kitchens' asserts a starting count the deck contradicts (two restaurants, neither paying). It does not print $750K, 300 or $500K: the ask gets placeholders, and the amount, milestone and date go to the founder as a question. B: right that an investor deck needs market arithmetic. The $8.2B figure is an unsourced lifted total, so it is not printed. It proposes customers times price with the kitchen count as a placeholder to source, or two facts left unmultiplied. C: declined as written. 'Only' needs a prior-art check and 'AI-native' is a consultant word, so the plain verbs line on slide 1 stays. D: declined. A grid in which the company wins every row is a tick grid. It keeps alternatives by kind and adds a concede-then-claim answer about the chains' systems, with a placeholder if the founder has not given the reason. E: declined. The deck's own strip lists the report as in build, so it cannot lead and cannot be stated in the present tense. It may appear as what the product is built to do, with no result attached. F: taken, and slide 4 is recorded under what already works. It also records what else works (claim headlines, the founder's own numbers, a price on the slide, the stage said once) so the next draft keeps it. It then gives the next headline outline with [NEED: ...] placeholders and a 'Numbers to find' list, asks five or fewer questions that only the founder can answer, and invents no numbers. It tells the founder plainly which points were sound advice about form and which figures were illustrations.
